noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment, and that body water content and body temperature are both examples of homeostasis

primer.text: You already know that enzymes need the right conditions to work and that the body is full of feedback systems keeping things steady. This note names that idea — homeostasis — and walks through its two flagship examples in humans: holding temperature near a set point and balancing the water content of the blood through the kidneys.

lessons.title: Homeostasis and why the internal environment matters
lessons.opening: Homeostasis means keeping the conditions inside the body steady even when the outside world shifts. Enzymes and cells only work inside narrow ranges, so drifting too far in either direction becomes dangerous. Temperature and the water content of the blood are the two classic examples you need to quote in exams.
keyPoints: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment of the body constant within set limits.
It matters because enzymes and cells only function properly within narrow internal ranges.
If conditions drift beyond those limits the organism can die.
Body temperature and body water content are the two named examples of homeostatic control.

low.restatement: Homeostasis holds internal conditions steady — temperature near a set point and blood water balanced — so enzymes keep working.
low.analogy: It is the body's thermostat and water meter running at once, nudging levels back whenever they wander.
low.examPointer: Quote the two examples — temperature and water content — by name; questions usually ask for both.

medium.restatement: Set limits protect enzyme activity and cell function; sensors detect drift, control centres process it, and effectors restore the optimum.
medium.analogy: Picture a greenhouse: vents and heaters respond to sensors so seedlings never cook or freeze, whatever the weather outside.
medium.examPointer: Link failure to death explicitly — exceeding the limits means enzymes stop working, which examiners reward.

options.text: Keeping conditions inside the body steady within set limits
options.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of constant internal conditions.
The body cannot alter its surroundings; it regulates its own interior.
Growth is a different life process entirely.
Reproduction has nothing to do with internal regulation.

check.stem: Which pair names the two examples of homeostasis required by the specification?

options.explanation: Glucose control exists but the specification's pair is temperature and water content.

options.text: Body temperature and body water content
options.explanation: These are the two named homeostatic examples.
Both are responses, not the named homeostatic pair.
Real physiological variables but not the specification's pair.

check.stem: Why can drifting beyond homeostatic limits be fatal?

options.text: Because enzymes stop functioning properly outside narrow ranges
options.explanation: Enzyme activity depends on stable internal conditions.

options.text: Because the body immediately runs out of water
options.explanation: Water loss matters but the fatal mechanism is enzyme and cell failure.

options.text: Because receptors run out of stimuli
options.explanation: Receptors do not consume stimuli.
Effectors respond to instructions; this is not the lethal mechanism.

check.stem: Homeostatic control in humans is best described as which kind of process?

options.text: A conscious decision made by the thinking brain
options.explanation: You never consciously choose to regulate temperature or water.
Homeostasis runs automatically via the brain stem and spinal cord.

options.text: A learned habit trained over years
options.explanation: It is built in from birth, not learned.

options.text: A purely chemical process with no control step
options.explanation: Control systems with receptors and centres are involved.

check.stem: What happens to enzyme activity if the internal environment stays within its set limits?

options.explanation: Enzyme activity plateaus; limits prevent damage, not boost it.
That is the consequence of exceeding limits, not staying inside them.

options.text: It works at its optimum for the organism's cells
options.explanation: Stable conditions are exactly what optimal enzyme and cell function need.
Enzymes always depend on temperature; stability protects that dependence.

check.modelAnswer: The maintenance of steady internal conditions within narrow set limits.

check.stem: Name the brain region that monitors the temperature of the blood.
check.modelAnswer: The thermoregulatory centre, found at the base of the brain.

check.stem: Explain why any rise or fall in core temperature demands a co-ordinated response.
check.modelAnswer: Because a temperature shift of more than about two degrees can be fatal: enzymes would no longer function at their optimum, so cooling or heating responses must be coordinated quickly to bring the temperature back toward its set point.

check.stem: During a heatwave a walker sweats heavily for hours. Name the organ that will adjust the final water balance and outline what it can control.
check.modelAnswer: The kidneys adjust the balance: water lost through sweat and breathing cannot be controlled, so the kidneys vary how much water is reabsorbed from the filtrate, producing either dilute or concentrated urine to protect the blood's water content.

lessons.title: Controlling temperature and water content in humans
sourceHeadings: Control of body temperature in humans
Control of body water content in humans
lessons.opening: Human core temperature sits close to 37 °C, monitored by the thermoregulatory centre at the base of the brain. Water balance is managed differently: losses through breathing and sweating cannot be adjusted, so the kidneys fine-tune how much water the urine carries away. ADH is the hormone steering that reabsorption.
keyPoints: Core body temperature stays near 37 °C; a shift beyond about two degrees can be fatal.
The thermoregulatory centre at the brain's base monitors blood temperature and coordinates cooling or heating responses.
Temperature receptors in the skin send extra signals to that centre.
The kidneys adjust how much water is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the nephron's collecting ducts.
Too little blood water means more reabsorption and concentrated urine; too much means dilute urine — ADH controls the switch.

low.restatement: Breathing and sweating lose water regardless, so control sits in the kidneys: ADH decides how much filtrate water returns, setting urine volume and concentration.
low.analogy: ADH works like a tap on the drain — more hormone closes the tap for a small, concentrated trickle; less opens it for a copious, dilute flow.
low.examPointer: Always attach ADH to the collecting duct — naming the nephron structure earns the mark.

medium.restatement: Thermoregulation pairs blood-borne and skin receptors with brain coordination, while osmoregulation couples kidney reabsorption to ADH release, both restoring set points.
medium.analogy: One system is a thermostat with sensors in two rooms; the other is a reservoir engineer releasing or storing water to hold the level constant.
medium.examPointer: Contrast the two losses: lungs and skin are uncontrollable, urine is adjustable — that contrast is the question's core.

check.stem: At approximately what core temperature is human blood held?

options.explanation: The core is kept close to 37 °C.
That is five degrees low; enzymes would struggle.
That is dangerously high and outside the limits.
Room temperature is not body temperature.

check.stem: Which water loss can the body actually control?

options.explanation: Lung loss is unavoidable.
Sweating serves temperature control; its water cost is not adjustable.
The kidneys control urine volume, making this the adjustable loss.
Tears are negligible and not a named control route.

check.stem: Where in the nephron is water reabsorbed from the filtrate?

options.explanation: Reabsorption happens specifically from the collecting ducts.
The bladder stores urine; it does not reabsorb water.
The urethra only carries urine out.
Sweat glands are skin structures outside the nephron entirely.

check.stem: When blood water falls too low, what does the body do?

options.text: Reabsorbs more water, producing a small volume of concentrated urine
options.explanation: More reabsorption conserves water and concentrates the urine.

options.text: Reabsorbs less water, producing dilute urine
options.explanation: That response would worsen the shortage.
Urine production continues, just reduced in volume.

options.text: Increases sweating to cool the blood
options.explanation: Sweating would lose still more water.

check.stem: Which hormone controls how much water the kidneys reabsorb?

options.explanation: ADH controls the reabsorption of water in the nephron.
Insulin manages blood glucose, not water.
Adrenaline prepares the body for emergencies.
FSH acts in the reproductive system.

check.stem: State where the thermoregulatory centre is located.
check.modelAnswer: At the base of the brain.

check.stem: Name the hormone that controls water reabsorption and the structure where it acts.
check.modelAnswer: ADH, acting on the collecting ducts of the nephron.

check.stem: Explain why water lost through the lungs cannot be regulated by the body.
check.modelAnswer: Breathing must continue constantly to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, so the water vapour exhaled with each breath is an unavoidable cost — unlike urine, its volume cannot be adjusted without stopping the gas exchange the body needs every second.

check.stem: A patient drinks a very large volume of water in a short time. Describe what their kidneys should produce and name the hormone change involved.
check.modelAnswer: With blood water too high, less water is reabsorbed from the filtrate, so the kidneys produce a large volume of dilute urine; ADH levels fall, opening the collecting-duct tap so the excess water leaves the body.

glossary.definition: The maintenance of steady internal conditions within narrow set limits despite external change.
The region at the base of the brain that monitors blood temperature and coordinates heating or cooling responses.
The nephron structure from which water is reabsorbed into the blood under ADH control.
The hormone that controls how much water the kidneys reabsorb, setting urine volume and concentration.
